articles.title: Drive-in cinemas are rare these days. But the last one in Melbourne’s north still draws a faithful crowd
articles.summary: The drive-in demands little of its audience. You can lie down, bring your dog and talk without fear of being hushed. Mridula Amin spent a night at one of the last of a dying breed. Between a funeral parlour and a sink factory, a queue of cars slowly disappears down a driveway.
body: “There’s something about watching a film under the stars, in the night air,” says Michael O’Neill, a car detailer who lives in Echuca, a five-hour return trip from the Coburg Drive-In.
At the peak of their popularity, there were more than 300 drive-in cinemas in Australia. Now, the Coburg Drive-In is the last one left within an hour of the Melbourne CBD.
O’Neil has been coming to the drive-in for 20 years, and when the light-up sign comes into view, it’s not unlike the feeling of coming home. He visits monthly.

People back home have often jeered, telling him it’s a waste of time. But O’Neill finds the traditional cinema experience lacklustre, “sat in a dark room, with phones buzzing and people talking”. He wants to live the drive-in experience while he can.

articles.title: ‘One Battle After Another’ and ‘Marty Supreme’ Take Top Honors at Location Managers Guild International Awards
articles.summary: The LGMI Awards were handed out on Saturday night and honor the use of filming locations across motion pictures, television, commercials, film commissions, and special achievement categories. Paul Thomas Anderson’s “One Battle After Another” won outstanding
body: “One Battle After Another” and “Marty Supreme” took top honors at the Location Managers Guild International (LMGI) LMGI Awarda.
Four-time Emmy-winning director and writer Vince Gilliga received the Eva Monley Award for his dedication to storytelling through location over his career and his most recent work on “Pluribus.”
Mike Fantasia, location manager of films including “Top Gun: Maverick,” “Killers of the Flower Moon” and “Spider-Man: Homecoming” was presented the Lifetime Achievement Award.

“Celebrating our LMGI winners was a truly remarkable experience,” Nancy Haecker, LMGI Awards Chair, said. “The ceremony was a powerful celebration of achievement, filled with inspiring moments and well-deserved recognition, beautifully capped by the genius of Vince Gilligan. Each of this year’s winners is incredibly deserving, and it was a distinct privilege to honor their talent, dedication, and outstanding contributions to our industry.”

articles.title: Dale Morris, Titan of Nashville Management Who Forged Superstar Careers for Kenny Chesney and Alabama, Dies at 89
articles.summary: Dale Morris, one of the leading names in the ranks of Nashville music managers, who helped build up superstar careers for the group Alabama and then Kenny Chesney nearly from scratch, died Friday at 89. A representative said Morris died in his sleep.
body: Lightning struck twice for Morris, as he oversaw the rise of Chesney from a country also-ran into the genre’s most reliable stadium-filler, who was named Entertainer of the Year four times in the 2000s by both the CMAs and ACMs, and who has enjoyed 32 No. 1 Billboard country smashes.
Other artists Morris steered included Old Dominion, Ricky Van Shelton, Jerry Lee Lewis and his very first management client going back into the late ’60s, Bobby “Crash” Craddock.

Said Higham, “He was larger than life, and never met a dream he couldn’t build. Dale Morris gave me my first internship, and I never wanted to go anywhere else. He saw things in people, in me, in Kenny, and inspired everyone to reach beyond what we thought possible. Maybe it’s how much he loved life, loved his family, loved us.”

Chesney devoted significant passages in his 2025 book, “Heart Life Music,” to describing his relationship with Morris, which came about from him being a huge fan of Alabama and discovering there was a man behind the scenes making it happen.

articles.title: Davis 'grateful' for support over cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The Office star was appearing at convention in London, less than two weeks after announcing her condition.
body: Actress Lucy Davis has told fans she is "grateful" for their support as she made an appearance at a London sci-fi convention, following the recent revelation she has incurable breast cancer.

Davis, who was on a panel to talk about her role in the 2004 zombie-comedy Shaun of the Dead, told an audience of hundreds of people about the interactions she had enjoyed with the film's fans during the event.

"It's like this whole second family you never knew you had, everyone is like a community, friendly, supportive of not only us but you guys and each other," she said. "We need a bit more niceness in the world, so I'm grateful."
It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.

articles.title: ‘Embryonic’: lost novel by French film-maker Éric Rohmer is republished
articles.summary: English translation of Élisabeth, the New Wave director’s 1946 book about young lovers in prewar Paris, receives rave reviews as precursor to auteur’s cinematic work. In the dog days of the second world war, 24-year-old Maurice Schérer wrote a tale of young lovers in prewar small-town France.
body: Now – eight decades on from its first publication, 16 years on from its author’s death – Élisabeth belatedly returns from the cold. Republished in an English-language translation by Aaron Kerner, Rohmer’s book has been greeted with glowing reviews, hailed as a lost modernist classic and a crucial origin story for the award-winning director of Claire’s Knee, The Green Ray and My Night at Maud’s. “It would be a rewarding, exciting read even if the identity of its author were unfamiliar,” wrote Richard Brody in the New Yorker. The fact that it’s by Rohmer? That’s the icing on the cake.

“On the one hand, to be honest, the book is a footnote,” says the novelist André Aciman, a longtime Rohmer fan who wrote the foreword to the new edition. “But it is also embryonic and full of Rohmerian moments. It takes on all the themes that will become more developed, complex and impactful in his films.”

articles.title: Blue plaque unveiled at home of Paddington creator
articles.summary: Chairman of the Haslemere Society, Chris Harrison, says it was a day where "friends were reunited".
body: The unveiling of a blue plaque at the former Surrey home of Paddington Bear creator Michael Bond was a "lovely" occasion with an unexpected surprise, the organiser has said.

Bond, who died in 2017 at the age of 91, moved to Fairacre in Haslemere in 1968, where he spent the next 10 years writing several Paddington books alongside the scripts for the original television series.
The unveiling on Saturday took place with the permission of current owners, Steph and Neil Stephenson, and was attended by Bond's daughter, Karen Jankel, who presented them with a special gift.
"It was the [Paddington] Bear that was Karen's as a child," Haslemere Society chairman Chris Harrison said.

articles.title: ‘Spa Weekend’ Review: Leslie Mann and Isla Fisher Go Underserved in a Lukewarm Bath of a Comedy
articles.summary: Anna Faris and Michelle Buteau also star in the film by 'Bad Moms' directors Jon Lucas and Scott Moore, about four childhood friends on a birthday trip that spirals out of control.
body: Have you ever had the experience of booking a trip that promised to be a blissful getaway, only to find once there that you’re having…not the worst time, but definitely a disappointing one? That the food that looked so pretty online tastes bland in person, that the overstuffed pillows give you neck pains, that — come to think of it — there’s not really that much to do at this resort beyond linger beside a lukewarm pool?

Along with her for the ride are her two childhood besties — sweet-natured Sophie ( Anna Faris ), who’s withering under a boss so spoiled he can’t even buy his own Skittles, and hot-tempered Coco ( Michelle Buteau ), who’s working through a painful divorce while stubbornly not working through the anger management issues that led to it.

articles.title: Nigel Havers: ‘My biggest disappointment? Not playing James Bond’
articles.summary: The actor on mucking out pigs as a teenager, an apology to his first wife and what makes him cry all the time. Born in London, Nigel Havers, 74, was Bafta-nominated for his 1981 role in Chariots of Fire. His other films include A Passage to India and Empire of the Sun.
body: What is your greatest fear? Every actor has the same fear – ie, you’re never going to work again.
What is your earliest memory? Being in a pram in London and there being a road accident ahead and saying to my mother, “Go quickly, I want to see what’s happened.”
Which living person do you most admire, and why? The king – because he’s been through quite a bit and I think he’s come out the other side brilliantly.
What is the trait you most deplore in others? When they don’t tell the truth.

articles.title: Mark Ruffalo Rejects Paramount’s Claim His Anti-Merger Comments Were “Antisemitic”: “My Views Should Never Be Interpreted as Hostility Toward Jewish People”
articles.summary: The actor and staunch opponent to the David Ellison-led studio's $111 billion deal for Warner Bros. recently took aim at Ellison's father Larry Ellison and his company Oracle's ties to the Israeli military.
body: Mark Ruffalo is rejecting Paramount ‘s claim that his recent comments highlighting the role Larry Ellison’s Oracle played in the Israel-Gaza war were “antisemitic.”

Ruffalo, a staunch opponent to Paramount’s $111 billion deal for Warner Bros., had recently shared on social media a clip from 2024 of former Oracle chief Safra Catz talking about “profoundly scary technologies” Oracle had built as Catz was speaking about Oracle’s tech in relation to the Israel-Gaza war. Ruffalo went on to call the war a “genocide” that “was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.”

He added in his Instagram story that these “profoundly scary technologies” “will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world” and criticized the planned Paramount-WB merger, saying moguls “are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.”
Paramount issued a lengthy reply in which the company called for the temperature of the debate to be lowered and called Ruffalo’s remarks “antisemitic.”
